  1. Know yourself. Think about what you like, what you don't and what works better for you. Don't just use general instructions about learning process, create your own best way to learn English.
  2. Check your environment. Is it good enough or maybe you need to change something?
  3. Ask yourself why are you doing something and what you will get from doing it and other questions that will help you to understand is that material important enough to spend time on it
  4. Choose your X target and try to focus on it. Do not spend much effort doing all related staff like Y,Z,etc..

  2. Short term goals: “Easy peasy.” Make it SMALL and EASY for EVERYDAY use.
  
  IMPORTANT: a) Chose a time and a place: To be consistent, daily, uninterrupted, and concentrate the most.
  
  3. Celebrate by: a.) dopamine=feel good, to do it again.
  b.) reward=give yourself another longer goal.

  These are fantastic tips! One piece of advice I always give my students is to ask the question, "How do I say this in English" as often as they can every day.   I'm a native speaker, but still get a lot out of your videos - especially the vocabulary.
  
  Not sure if it helps anyone - when I was in school, the trick I was taught (and still use to this day) for "there/their/they're" was to drop the T's and expand the contraction. 
  
  there => here => it's used for locations... over there
  their => heir  => it's used for possession or ownership... in their house
  they're => they are => it's a contraction... they are home
  
  they're home over there in their house

  Just a few notes on the word ‘goner’
  
  I’m pretty certain the word ‘goner’ derives from the word ‘gone’ which means to… disappear, no longer exist, or to have been moved or move itself to a different location. 
  So, to be a ‘goner’ would mean that you will disappear, or cease to exist.
  
  However, goner can also be used in different contexts, though rarely. Sometimes, for example in sport, people can say “I thought we were goners in the first half, but somehow we managed to get the win” Meaning they thought they were going to lose in the first half of the game.

    ↳ **@Hootiefish** (👍0 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jnJHFaIPjgs&lc=UgzeW-1rAO8dzuVnbFx4AaABAg.9OxquZm4jEK9OzFc0sx_CM
      Not entirely sure if you’re looking for the pronunciation of the word murder or for context.
      But I’ll try my best to help with giving you context.
      
      The word murder can be used a few ways. For starters, as I’m sure you know, is a word that means the killing of a human, animal, or even plant in some contexts.
      You can murder a human and be sent to jail.
      You can murder an ant by stepping on it and crushing it.
      You can even murder a plant by ripping it up or not watering it, although the word murder here is used lightly.
      
      Even though you can use the word murder for the killing of an animal or plant, using it for these scenarios is a bit overkill. Murder is usually used for the killing of a human.
      
      You can even use murder as a threat,
      “I’m going to murder you”
      This can be used in a serious context, if you actually want to kill that person, or it can be used lightly in a joking way.
      If someone spilt their drink on your important notes you could say “I’m going to murder you.”
      
      Hope that wasn’t too confusing and hopefully it helped somehow.
      
      Also if you were looking for pronunciation, it sort of just sounds like it’s spelt. Mur-der.

  Is it "politically correct" to say "Could you please hand the salad over to me"? e.g during a dinner with father and mother-in-law? Or would it be seen rude? Of course I know it's much easier and appropriate to say "Could you pass...." but I'm just looking for an alternative.
    ↳ **@Hootiefish** (👍1 · 2021-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jnJHFaIPjgs&lc=UgxtiKqS5lTxZT_3oYl4AaABAg.9OyQWxs0eta9OzGZULWhrc
      Hi! Native English speaker from Australia here so I hope you can trust my judgement.
      
      Saying “could you please hand the salad over to me” is perfectly fine and would not be seen as rude or offensive in any way shape or form. It’s equal to saying “Could you please pass the salad over to me” 
      You could even say “Could you please hand me the salad” 
      
      Honestly, I would much prefer if someone asked me
      “Could you please hand me the salad”
      Than
      “Could you please give me the salad”
      
      It’s only offensive when used as “hand it over” or “hand it to me”.
      
      Hope this helps!

  Another point is also important: repetition. If you read words only once they don't stay in your memory long. But already the old Romans knew the secret: "Repetitio est mater studiorum." **@Alexandra66** (👍3 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CVHg6k6sRjc&lc=Ugzl1BvKLLTNMCuUpp94AaABAg
  الفيديو يلخص 25 كلمة إنجليزية أكاديمية مفيدة لطلاب الجامعة، أو الإعداد لامتحاني IELTS أو TOEFL:
   * Arbitrary [00:17]: بناءً على الرغبة أو الصدفة بدلاً من السبب. تتضمن التعبيرات الشائعة "قرار اعتباطي" أو "خيار اعتباطي" أو "تاريخ اعتباطي".
   * Inherent [00:48]: موجود كجزء طبيعي أو أساسي من شيء ما، وغالبًا ما يستخدم كصفة نسبية (على سبيل المثال، "مشكلة متأصلة"، "خطر متأصل").
   * Notwithstanding [01:31]: على الرغم من الحقيقة أو الشيء المذكور.
   * Norm [02:16]: معيار مقبول أو طريقة للتصرف أو فعل الأشياء يتفق عليها معظم الناس (على سبيل المثال، "الأعراف الاجتماعية"، "الأعراف السياسية").
   * Straightforward [02:39]: سهل الفهم أو بسيط (على سبيل المثال، "مهمة مباشرة"، "تعليمات مباشرة").
   * Furthermore [03:09]: بالإضافة إلى ذلك أو الأهم من ذلك، غالبًا ما تستخدم في بداية الجملة لإضافة معلومات.
   * Enormous [03:32]: كبير للغاية، يستخدم لإضافة التأكيد (على سبيل المثال، "تأثير هائل"، "فرق هائل"، "كمية هائلة").
   * Precise [05:40]: دقيق وصحيح.
   * Deviate [06:09]: تغيير عن الطريقة المعتادة أو الذهاب في اتجاه مختلف، وغالبًا ما يتبع بـ "من".
   * Explicit [06:47]: واضح ودقيق (على سبيل المثال، "توجيهات صريحة"، "تعليمات صريحة"، "تحذير صريح").
   * Phenomenon [07:11]: شيء موجود ويمكن الشعور به أو رؤيته أو تذوقه، خاصة شيء غريب أو غير عادي.
   * Mediate [07:55]: التحدث إلى شخصين منفصلين أو مجموعات متورطة في خلاف لإيجاد حل، وغالبًا ما يتبع بـ "بين".
   * Undergo [08:33]: تجربة شيء غير سار أو شيء ينطوي على تغيير (على سبيل المثال، "الخضوع لعملية جراحية"، "الخضوع لتحول").
   * Likewise [09:27]: بنفس الطريقة؛ يمكن استخدامه أيضًا بشكل غير رسمي بمعنى "أنا أيضًا".
   * Via [10:13]: حرف جر بمعنى "المرور عبر مكان أو التوقف فيه في طريقك إلى مكان آخر" (للسفر) أو "استخدام آلة أو نظام أو شخص معين لإرسال أو استقبال شيء ما".
   * Finite [10:50]: وجود حد أو نهاية (على سبيل المثال، "كمية محدودة"، "مورد محدود").
   * Ideology [11:21]: مجموعة من المعتقدات أو المبادئ، خاصة تلك القائمة على نظام سياسي أو حزب أو منظمة.
   * Innovate [11:53]: إدخال تغييرات أو أفكار جديدة، غالبًا في سياق التكنولوجيا.
   * Confer [12:33]: تبادل الأفكار حول موضوع معين، غالبًا للتوصل إلى قرار، وعادة ما يتبع بـ "مع".
   * Widespread [13:16]: موجود أو يحدث في أماكن كثيرة و / أو بين كثير من الناس، وغالبًا ما يستخدم كصفة نسبية (على سبيل المثال، "دعم واسع النطاق"، "فساد واسع النطاق").
   * Rigid [13:43]: لا يسمح بأي تغيير (مثل القواعد أو الجدول الزمني) أو صلب / ثابت (غير قادر على الانحناء أو التحرك).
   * Reluctant [14:14]: غير راغب في فعل شيء ما وبالتالي بطيء في القيام به، وغالبًا ما يتبع بـ "إلى". تتضمن عائلة الكلمة "reluctantly" (ظرف) و "reluctance" (اسم).
   * Justify [14:48]: إعطاء أو أن تكون سببًا وجيهًا لشيء ما (على سبيل المثال، "الغاية تبرر الوسيلة").
   * Radical [15:20]: الاعتقاد أو التعبير عن الاعتقاد بضرورة وجود تغيير اجتماعي أو سياسي كبير أو متطرف، يستخدم لإضافة التأكيد (على سبيل المثال، "تغيير جذري"، "وجهات نظر جذرية").
   * Whereas [16:00]: أداة ربط تستخدم لمقارنة ومقارنة ميزات الأشخاص أو الأشياء المختلفة.

**@ZestonN** (👍2 · 2026-01-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y0em7H1JIh4&lc=UgwIh9vfRqulO3F6-vB4AaABAg
  If you're having trouble reading Turkish (Turkiç), you're probably reading it in a difficult script. 
  
  There's a Latin-script version of Turkish; A Cyrillic version of Turkish; and an Abjad version of Turkish.
  
  The Latin version uses a lot of extra characters found in French and Polish.
  
  So, I would recommend using the Cyrillic alphabet. It's more uniformed and has a clearer "One Character, One Sound" Format.
  
  When you feel comfortable reading Turkish in one script, try replacing words you already know into new scripts. This will get your mind use to different scripts; making transitions to other languages like Arabic, Ukranian, or even Japanese easier.
  
  Japanese uses three scripts, interchangeably, and regularly. So practicing a language that has three optional scripts, opens a multitude of pathways to other languages. 🙂

**@sheedcainiste2061** (👍3 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gK2Ut6_dBdw&lc=Ugx0hh-Qa161MFVMUDh4AaABAg
  Hi , I need some explanations . I have been studying at C1 level for a year but when I do CAE tests, I keep failing . It seems like whatever efforts I put into learning, I will always be stuck at B2 . Is there something wrong with me?
    ↳ **@EnglishwithIssy [channel author]** (👍3 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gK2Ut6_dBdw&lc=Ugx0hh-Qa161MFVMUDh4AaABAg.ACW6PfYChTWAEwRNtYRAAf
      Hi friend, there's nothing wrong with you, but language learning is a process that takes a long time.
      
      To move forward, you need to analyse your past papers, be a detective and find out WHY you're not passing.
      
      Is it reading, listening, speaking?
      
      Then, what specifically is the problem, is it use of english part 4? Are your wrong answers grammar-related or vocabulary? Is it phrasal verbs or conditionals?
      
      Once you know exactly what your weaknesses are, you wan work specifically on them, and you'll see progress!

      IELTS Speaking — 7 Day Crash List  
      Exam in 7-8 days? Prep ONLY these 12 topics. They cover 80% of 2026 tests.
      
      MUST-PREPARE CUE CARDS — Part 2:
      
      Topic: People
      1. Describe a person who helped you achieve something
      2. Describe a person who has had a significant influence on your life
      3. Describe a person who encouraged you to achieve a goal
      4. Describe a time you helped someone you didn’t know
      
      Topic: Places/Travel
      5. Describe a memorable journey or trip
      6. Describe a crowded/noisy place you visited
      7. Describe a beautiful city you would like to visit in the future
      
      Topic: Technology/Skills/Decisions
      8. Describe a useful website or app
      9. Describe a piece of technology you find difficult to use
      10. Describe a difficult decision you made
      11. Describe a skill you want to learn
      12. Describe something you do to stay healthy
      
      MUST-PREPARE PART 1 TOPICS — 30 sec answers:
      Sleep, Apps, Technology, Food, Travel, Reading, Sports, Shopping, Friends, Family, Weekends, Music, Public transport, Weather
      
      Quick Tip: Prepare 3 stories only. Reuse them for all cards.  
      Structure: Past → Present → Future.  
      Words to use: Furthermore, In addition, However, Significant, Beneficial.
      
      7-Day Plan: 3 days = prep 3 stories. 1 day = mock test. 1 day = Part 1. 1 day = rest.  
      Don’t memorize full answers. Don’t say “I don’t know”.

  Hi Chris,
  
  I just wanted to share this with you as an update. Last week, on July 14th, I took the IELTS Academic UKVI exam with IDP here in Ankara, Turkey. My scores were: Listening 5.0, Reading 5.0, Writing 5.5, Speaking 7.0.
  
  I was so frustrated with those results that I retook the exam just a week later, on July 23rd. In between, I only prepared using your videos and a couple of other sources. What I realized was that during the first attempt, I wasn't really applying any strategy or technique — I was just answering questions blindly. Honestly, every section of this exam is tough, but Reading on its own can be genuinely brutal. This time around, I applied the techniques — especially in Reading, where I asked the text questions and actually hunted down the answers.
  
  My results from July 23rd: Reading 6.5, Listening 6.5, Writing 7.0, Speaking 6.0.
  
  As for Speaking — I had an Indian examiner this time, and even though I answered the questions fluently, I still ended up with a lower score. Honestly, the examiner phrased the questions with oddly inverted sentence structures, seemingly on purpose, and there's this stereotype that some Indian examiners aren't favorable toward Turkish candidates. I genuinely and seriously believe there was some subjectivity in that evaluation. Still, I won't be requesting a re-evaluation — the scores I ended up with were exactly what I needed anyway, so I'm satisfied.
  
  I actually discovered where I'd been going wrong through one comment I watched in your videos: it's not about solving more questions, it's about learning the TACTICS. And that one shift genuinely pulled my results up dramatically. The moment you said that using techniques matters more than just cramming in extra practice, I sat down and solved questions non-stop for 6 hours — and the outcome honestly shocked me.
  
  So, dear Chris, I really can't thank you enough. I do have a surprise planned for you as well, but I'll keep that under wraps for now.
  
  Warm regards and respect, from Ankara/Turkiye! 😇

    ↳ **@Ieltsadvantage [channel author]** (👍0 · 2026-08-07) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9hsQem11og&lc=Ugy8Fa6NuVrBsDtV8MR4AaABAg.A_6lvd3wfjlA_8HbJMusBR
      Hi there! A few "um," "uh," or brief pauses are completely normal and won't automatically lower your score. For Band 7, what matters most is that you can speak fluently, communicate your ideas clearly, and recover naturally after a short hesitation. It's only when hesitations are frequent or long enough to interrupt your fluency that they may affect your score.

      The rules say that r is silent at the end of a word (or before a consonant).  The word "more" ends with a vowel, because final "e" is silent in English (with a small number of exceptions, of course).  So although "more" ends with a vowel letter, it doesn't end with a vowel sound.  It would end with an r sound, if the r were pronounced, but that's disallowed by the rules.  Hence why "sore" sounds the same as "saw", and "floor" the same as "flaw", and all of them rhyme with "more".

**@kristensaenz6421** (👍0 · 2026-07-15) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K0xYMBmdUsI&lc=Ugy3eyliSkEH8Lb0u554AaABAg
  My question is why not pronounce the r? Why is it there if not to be pronounced. What is the history behind dropping the r sound sometimes and adding it where it doesnt exist? It is interesting how language develops and changes. Why do North Americans pronounce r?
    ↳ **@rp1692** (👍0 · 2026-07-22) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K0xYMBmdUsI&lc=Ugy3eyliSkEH8Lb0u554AaABAg.AZBL2L0uJJpAZK_v1iOcOZ
      Well, although it is not pronounced as an /r/, it does have an effect a lot of the time.  For instance, "moor" isn't pronounced the same as "moo".  "Burn" isn't pronounced the same as "bun".  "Darn" isn't "Dan".  So, the written r tells us that the vowel is pronounced differently.  Now, historically, I think it was in 19th century London that the practice of dropping /r/ arose.  It may even have been earlier than that.  But pronouncing /r/ is the older practice, so this is one area where American pronunciation is older.  Still, it is a myth that American pronunciation as a whole is older than British.  Changes have occurred in both British and American English over the centuries.  Plus, there are some Americans who drop their /r/s.  This used to be fairly common (for instance, President Franklin Roosevelt did it, as did many actors in "old" Hollywood between the wars).  Over time, nonrhotic pronunciations have declined in North America, while rhotic pronunciations have declined in England (they are still commonly encountered in Scotland, though).

      Historical reasons, like the "h" in "where" (some people pronounce the "h", but most don't) or the "gh" in "though" or the "k" in "knee" (it used to be pronounced, many centuries ago).  Furthermore, although the R is no longer pronounced as a proper R, it signals the quality of the preceding vowel.  So, while neither "ton" nor "torn" contains an /r/, the vowels of the two words are different, and the spelling reminds us of that.
